what_changed: Whole-code modernisation with no change of rule. Mostly capitalisation of nouns (1755 capitalises 'Wicket', 'Ball' and so on) and spelling ('in' -> 'inn'). The wording changes are: the ball stops being 'she'/'her' and becomes 'it' ('though she be struck' -> 'tho' it be struck'; 'before she touches ground' -> 'before it touches the Ground'); 'cast of a piece of money' -> 'Toss of a Piece of Money'; 'the either popping-crease' -> 'the other Popping-Crease'; 'then it's out' -> 'or else it's not out'; 'no person shall have the right to ask him' -> 'no Person shall have any Right to question him'; 'which design must be determined by the umpires' -> 'the same must be determined by the Umpires'. 'awing the game' in 1752 is an OCR misreading of 'giving'. Measurements are the same (3 ft 10 in, 22 yards, 22 in stumps, 6 in bail, 5-6 oz ball).
rationale: Rait Kerr (App. III) says the 1755 Laws 'are essentially the 1752 version in a slightly modernised form' and that the common code 'had not varied materially since 1744'. In ch.1 he names, as signs of 'gradual modernisation', 'Ye' becoming 'The' and 'the ball ceasing to be referred to as "She" or "Her"'. This event shows exactly that. No Rait Kerr serial falls between 1744 and 1771 (serials 1-21 are the 1744 baseline). The ACS transcription of 1755 matches the dataset's 1755 wording. The pronoun change has no effect on the rule; nor does 'question' for 'ask' (in both, no-one may challenge the umpire's no-ball call).
date_evidence: 1752 printing of the 1744 code vs 1755 booklet (advertised 15 May 1755, Rait Kerr App. III)
notes: 1752 OCR also has 'awing' for 'giving'; capitalisation differences are format only Corrected after verification: F2: Rait Kerr names the modernisation but not a cause; basis should be inferred.

what_changed: 'These laws are to the umpires jointly.' appears to be removed. It is still in the 1755 text, where it was printed together with the next sentence ('These Laws are to the Umpires jointly. ___ Each Umpire is the sole Judge...'). The segmenter treated it as part of that record.
rationale: The sentence is in the 1755 processed text and in the ACS 1755 transcription, so the removal is a sentence-splitting artefact.

what_changed: The 1755 opening block is dropped as a unit and its contents are reorganised under separate headings ('The BOWLING-CREASE', 'The POPPING-CREASE', 'The Party which goes from Home'). The block contained: the toss for pitching the first wicket ('determined by the Toss of a Piece of Money'), the popping-crease distance (3 ft 10 in), the 22-yard distance between wickets, and 'The Bowling-Creases must be cut in a direct Line from each Stump'. The measurements carry over unchanged. Two real policy changes are hidden in the removal: the toss for the pitch gives way to the visiting side's choice, and the bowling crease is redefined. Each is labelled in the event that adds the new heading.
rationale: Rait Kerr App. III states that the 1774 revision 'included radical modifications to both the sequence and the wording of the 1755 version'. The policy content is Rait Kerr serials 27 (choice of pitch and innings) and 28 (bowling crease 3 ft), for which he gives no cause.
date_evidence: 25 Feb 1774 (Rait Kerr serials 27, 28)

what_changed: Ball: 'must weigh between Five & Six Ounces' -> 'MUST not weigh less than five ounces and a half, nor more than five ounces and three quarters' (tolerance narrowed to 5.5-5.75 oz). New: 'It cannot be changed during the game, but with consent of both parties'. This replaces the umpires' duty 'To mark the Ball that it may not be changed', and the ball may now be changed by consent. The old record also carried the toss-up for choice of innings, which moved to the visiting-side rule.
rationale: Rait Kerr serial 25: 'The tolerance for the weight of the ball is reduced to be between 5½ and 5¾ ounces'. He gives no reason for this item. He says the 1774 changes overall 'were mainly directed towards the closer definition necessary for the more serious game in course of development' (ch.2), so the closer-definition reading is inferred. Numbers are confirmed by raw OCR ('five ounces and a half ... five ounces and three quarters') and by the ACS 1774 transcription.
date_evidence: 25 Feb 1774 (Rait Kerr serial 25)
notes: Also a relocation (split): The 1755 ball sentence and the following toss-for-innings sentence formed one block of the unheaded opening paragraph; in 1774 the ball gets its own heading 'The BALL' and the innings choice moves to the new visiting-side Law. Rule change kept as primary: weight limits narrowed from 5-6 oz to 5.5-5.75 oz and ball not to be changed without consent.

what_changed: Umpires' Laws rewritten. (1) 'Ten Minutes between each Hand' -> 'fifteen minutes between each innings'. (2) 'When both Umpires call Play three Times, 'tis at the Peril of giving the Game' -> 'when the umpire shall call play, the party refusing to play shall lose the match'. (3) 'are not to allow a fresh Man to play, on either Side, on any Account' dropped, and the hurt man now 'shall have his place in any part of that innings'. (4) Dropped: umpires' sole judgement of 'frivolous Delays' and 'Hurts', of 'Hindrances' (with the power to order a notch for hindrance), 'Each Umpire is the sole Judge ... at his own Wicket', 'he shall not be changed for another Umpire, without the Consent of both Sides', and 'When the four Balls are bowl'd, he is to call over'. (5) New: umpires are 'sole judges of fair and unfair play, and all disputes'; 'appealed to by one of the Players' -> 'by the adversaries'; the no-ball call moved here from the bowlers' Law ('the umpire, unasked, must call no ball'); and new 'If the strikers run a short notch, the umpire must call no notch'.
rationale: Rait Kerr serials 29 (interval 10 -> 15 minutes; 'Play' called once), 30 ('Short runs' specially referred to for the first time) and 23 (substitutes no longer prohibited) give no cause. Serials 24 (umpires changed by consent), 31 (call of 'Over') and 33 (each umpire at his own wicket) are among the 'five omissions from the previous code which may well have resulted from careless drafting' (ch.2; Rait Kerr's conjecture). The secondary label records that conjecture.
date_evidence: 25 Feb 1774 (Rait Kerr serials 23, 24, 29, 30, 31, 33)
notes: Also a relocation (merge): The 1755 umpires' Laws were printed as separate sub-lists ('These Laws are to the Umpires jointly' / 'These Laws are separately'); 1774 combines them into one 'The UMPIRES' Law, which also receives the bowler's no-ball call moved from the bowlers' Laws. Rule changes kept as primary: 15 instead of 10 minutes between innings, refusal to play after one call of play loses the match, 'call over' and ball-marking duties dropped, new short-notch call.

If one party beats the other in one innings, the notches in the first innings shall determine the bet. But if the party goes in a second time, then the bet must be determined by the number on the score.'
rationale: Rait Kerr ch.2: 'The 1774 Laws for betting were introduced to meet the changing requirements of the gamblers'. He quotes these three rules and links them to the growth of high-stakes matches and to a 1774 Chelmsford Chronicle attack on 'excessive gaming'.

It matches Rait Kerr's note that Blake's c.1786 edition has 'a minor alteration ... in a rule for the Single Wicket game' (App. III). Rait Kerr's chronology has no serial for this and gives no cause.

what_changed: New BAT Law: 'Must not exceed four inches and one quarter in the widest part.' (no width limit before)
rationale: Rait Kerr serials 22 and 26: the Hambledon committee limited the width to 4¼ in on 25 Sept 1771, and the 1774 code confirms it. In ch.2 he quotes Nyren: a player named White, of Ryegate, 'brought a bat to a match, which being the width of the stumps, effectually defended his wicket from the bowler: and in consequence, a law was passed limiting the future width of the bat to four and a quarter inches'.
date_evidence: Hambledon decision 25 Sept 1771; in the code 25 Feb 1774

what_changed: Stumps: 'must be Twenty-Two Inches long, and the Bail Six Inches' -> 'Must be twenty-two inches, and the bail six inches long; but by a subsequent meeting it is settled for to use three stumps instead of two, to each wicket, and the two bails not to exceed six inches.' This introduces the three-stump wicket and two bails.
rationale: Rait Kerr serial 34 (c.1775): the three-stump wicket followed the Hambledon v Kent single-wicket match of 22-23 May 1775, where Lumpy's balls passed three times between Small's two stumps. He quotes Nyren: 'it was considered to be a hard thing upon the bowler that his straightest balls should be thus sacrificed; the number of the stumps was in consequence increased from two to three'. Two bails are serial 36: first referred to in the Maidstone edition c.1786, no cause given. The 1774 code itself (ACS) has two stumps and one bail.
date_evidence: Third stump c.1775 (serial 34; first in a dated edition in Wallis 1785, serial 35); two bails c.1786 (serial 36). Dataset '1774' text is a later printing (Blake's Maidstone edition c.1786 by Rait Kerr's App. III description); the 1774 code was adopted 25 Feb 1774.

His general statement that the 1774 changes were 'mainly directed towards the closer definition necessary for the more serious game' supports the closer-definition reading by inference.

what_changed: New heading 'The POPPING-CREASE': 'Must be three feet ten inches from the wickets; and the wickets must be opposite to each other, at the distance of twenty-two yards.' The values are those of the 1755 opening block (3 ft 10 in; 22 yards), now under their own heading.

what_changed: Strikers' Laws rewritten as a list 'The STRIKER is out ... Or if ...'. The main change is the first L.B.W. law: 'Or if the striker puts his leg before the wicket with a design to stop the ball, and actually prevents the ball from hitting his wicket by it.' Other changes: '(but not Arms)' -> '(but not wrists)' in the catch rule and 'of the catcher' added. 'nipp'd up ... before it came to the Wicket' -> 'struck up, and he wilfully strike it again'. Run out may now be made 'with the ball in hand', and if the bail is off 'a stump must be struck out of the ground by the ball'. 'he that returns' -> 'he that has left the wicket'. 'unless ask'd by the Bowler, or Wicket-Keeper' -> 'unless at the request of the opposite party'. The old 'he may go where he pleases till the next Ball' becomes 'the strikers need not keep within their ground till the umpire has called play; but if the player goes out of his ground, with an intent to run before the ball is delivered, the bowler may put him out'. Dropped: the striker's partner placing 'his Body any where within the Swing of the Bat' to hinder a catch, the umpires ordering a notch for designed crossing, and 'The Bail hanging on one Stump ... it's not out'. The text also says 'either of the bails' (two bails).
rationale: Rait Kerr serial 32b: 'The first specific "L.B.W." Law is introduced'. He reports that 'Silver Billy' Beldham remembered it 'as a cure for the "shabby" methods adopted by the batsmen', and notes that the 1744 Laws already let umpires judge 'standing unfair to strike'. So the cause is Beldham's claim, reported by Rait Kerr. The other rewrites have no stated cause (Rait Kerr gives only the general 'closer definition' aim of 1774), hence the secondary UNCATEGORISED.
date_evidence: 25 Feb 1774 (serial 32b); 'either of the bails' wording c.1786 (serial 36). Dataset '1774' text is a later printing (Blake's Maidstone edition c.1786 by Rait Kerr's App. III description); the 1774 code was adopted 25 Feb 1774.

what_changed: A block of strikers' provisions counted as a new pseudo-Law. It contains three new 1788 provisions. (1) Obstruction: 'Or, if under pretence of running a Notch, or otherwise, either of the Strikers prevent a Ball from being caught, the Striker of the Ball is out.' This replaces 'Or if he runs out of his ground to hinder a catch' and the old licence that 'it is lawful for the strikers to hinder its being catched'. (2) L.B.W. rewritten: 'If with his foot or leg he stops the Ball, which the Bowler in the opinion of the Umpire at the Bowler's Wicket shall have pitched in straight line to the Wicket, and would have hit it' (old: 'puts his leg before the wicket with a design to stop the ball'). (3) 'When a Ball is caught, no Notch to be reckoned. When a Striker is run out, the Notch they were running for is not to be reckoned.' Also 'before it has lain still' -> 'while in play' for handling the ball, and the ball in the bowler's or keeper's hands 'is considered as no longer in Play'.
rationale: Rait Kerr ch.2 on the 1788 code: 'The new code contained only four new provisions—of these, three were closer definitions of the Laws dealing with "L.B.W.," the obstruction of a catch, and for the disallowance of runs in the case of a catch or a run out—all in strict keeping with Hambledon's established conception of the game as one deserving more detailed legislation than had hitherto been provided.' Serials 41 (runs on a catch/run out), 43 (L.B.W. restricted to a ball 'pitched in a straight line to the wicket') and 38 (obstruction law, first in the second Maidstone edition c.1787 'in identical wording to that later used in the first M.C.C. Code'). Rait Kerr states the purpose of these specific provisions (closer definition). L.B.W. now turns on where the ball pitched rather than the batsman's design.
date_evidence: 30 May 1788 (serials 41, 43); obstruction wording c.1787 (serial 38). First M.C.C. code, 30 May 1788 (Britcher; Rait Kerr App. III notes Britcher may have included later changes).

what_changed: Six strikers' provisions relocated. Substantive wording changes: handling the ball 'before it has lain still' -> 'while in play'. 'that is put down' -> 'which is put down'; 'Single-Wicket' -> 'single Wicket'.
rationale: Rait Kerr has no serial for the 'in play' wording. It belongs to the 1788 code, whose new provisions he describes as closer definitions giving the game 'more detailed legislation'. Applied to these clauses, that is an inference. The 'in play' concept replaces a vaguer test ('lain still') without changing the rule's purpose.

He conjectures that this 1774 omission 'may well have resulted from careless drafting'. Reading the 1788 restoration as a correction of that omission is an inference. The new mechanism (refer an unseen catch to the other umpire; the bowler's-end umpire first) has no stated cause, hence secondary UNCATEGORISED.

rationale: Rait Kerr gives no serial or cause for this change. He says the betting Laws themselves 'were introduced to meet the changing requirements of the gamblers' (1774) and describes stakes rising up to 1790. Attributing the 1788 change of default settlement to the same purpose is an inference. The provision only concerns how bets are settled, so ECONOMY is the only plausible domain.

law_title: THE PARTY WHICH GOES FROM HOME
what_changed: Visiting side: wording the same, but the third-place toss is now 'for the pitching of the Wickets' (was 'of the First Wicket'). New rule: 'It shall not be lawful for either Party during a Match without the consent of the other to alter the Ground, by rolling, watering, covering, mowing, or beating; this rule is not meant to prevent a Striker from beating the ground with his Bat near where he stands during the Innings, or to prevent the Bowler from filling up holes, watering his ground, or using Sawdust, &c. when the ground is wet.'
rationale: Rait Kerr serial 40 (30 May 1788): 'For the first time a Law provides for rolling, watering, covering, mowing and beating of the pitch during a match by mutual consent'. In ch.2 he calls it 'surely the earliest sign of the now accepted principle that bad conditions make for bad cricket; doubtless it reflected the tremendous advance made in bowling technique, and thereby in batting, by such players as David Harris'. That is his own inference ('surely', 'doubtless'), so the basis is inferred.

what_changed: Striker-out list. Hit wicket reintroduced in new words: 'Or if in striking at the Ball he hits down his [Wicket]'. Catch rule 'upon his Hands' -> 'upon his hand', 'though if he hugged' (OCR) -> 'although it be hugged'. The old L.B.W. rule, 'it is lawful for the strikers to hinder its being catched', and the old run-out wording leave this list; their replacements are in the new block (see the event adding the obstruction law).

It had disappeared in 1774 (serial 32a), which he conjectures 'may well have resulted from careless drafting', so restoring it corrects a drafting omission (conjecture). The 'at any other time while the Ball is in play' extension of stumping has no serial or stated cause, hence secondary UNCATEGORISED.
date_evidence: 30 May 1788 (serial 42); c.1786 in the Maidstone edition (serial 37)

what_changed: Ball: new 'At the beginning of each innings either party may call for a new ball.' The 1788 clause 'it cannot be changed during the Game, but by the consent of both Parties' is dropped, and 'nor more than' -> 'and not more than'.

In ch.2 he says the early M.C.C.'s major alterations were 'confined to giving assistance to the bowler by increasing the size of the wicket, and by allowing a new ball at the start of each innings'. Serial 47: 'A new ball may be demanded by either side at the start of each innings.'

what_changed: Striker-out list re-segmented (Pocock prints it as one ';or,' chain). Variants: 'and either wilfully strike it again' (was 'he wilfully strikes'), 'takes up his ball' (was 'the Ball').
rationale: Rait Kerr serial 49a (1798): 'A new Law provides a penalty of 5 runs if the fieldsman stops a ball with his hat. No doubt the adoption of the top hat as part of the usual attire of the players led to this introduction.' Serial 49b: 'Dead ball' is used for the first time in this Law. 'No doubt' marks his own inference. Serial 45 (1798, 'substitutes in the field is recognised without restriction') covers the stand-out rule and gives no cause, hence secondary UNCATEGORISED. 'either' and 'his ball' are Pocock's variants (ACS's 1809 Wallis text has 'he' and 'the Ball').

what_changed: Old Law 50 -> Law 18: umpires call 'Time' and remove the bails at every interval, the end of each day and the end of the match.
